{
  "question_intent": "Discuss competitive dynamics, balance sheet demand, and product margins in CIB, and the impact of US and UK capital regulations.",
  "main_topics": ["Competitive Dynamics", "Balance Sheet Demand", "Product Margins", "CIB", "US and UK Capital Regulations"],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "Medium",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": false,
  "contains_forward_guidance": false,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "Pam, there's been a lot of column inches devoted to capital rejigging in the UK, and you're running a higher capital ratio than most of the banks that we look at. I wonder whether you'd talk a little bit about competitive dynamics in the CIB in particular. There's a lot written about de-regulation in the US, but in Q1 we did see a lot of banks missing on CET1. Granted, you were not one of them. And so if you could just talk a little bit about balance sheet demand and what's happening to product margins in CIB in particular, given that there's a lot of interest in whether those are destined to come down as US banks deploy the capital that we think they'll now see released. Thanks.",
  "answer_quote": "So the demand coming from the US or UK, of course, we are a participant, but we take our share and no more. Our reliance on growth is there, but not as much as some of the peers. For us, the big demand in growth is coming from Asia, where demand was really low, but we expect more to come through, particularly through commercial banking clients, larger clients. And in those areas and in those markets, we don't see pressure on our margins. It's just where that growth is coming. In terms of CET1, we are comfortable with the operating range we have, but we'll wait to see what happens from a regulation in a UK perspective. And in terms of the work we are doing on balance sheet velocity, that would just give us an ability to be able to participate more without having that increase in RWAs and follow-through. I think we should all be pleased. data.question_intent: Discuss competitive dynamics, balance sheet demand, and product margins in CIB, and the impact of US and UK capital regulations.
data.question_quote: Pam, there's been a lot of column inches devoted to capital rejigging in the UK, and you're running a higher capital ratio than most of the banks that we look at. I wonder whether you'd talk a little bit about competitive dynamics in the CIB in particular. There's a lot written about de-regulation in the US, but in Q1 we did see a lot of banks missing on CET1. Granted, you were not one of them. And so if you could just talk a little bit about balance sheet demand and what's happening to product margins in CIB in particular, given that there's a lot of interest in whether those are destined to come down as US banks deploy the capital that we think they'll now see released. Thanks.
data.answer_quote: So the demand coming from the US or UK, of course, we are a participant, but we take our share and no more. Our reliance on growth is there, but not as much as some of the peers. For us, the big demand in growth is coming from Asia, where demand was really low, but we expect more to come through, particularly through commercial banking clients, larger clients. And in those areas and in those markets, we don't see pressure on our margins. It's just where that growth is coming. In terms of CET1, we are comfortable with the operating range we have, but we'll wait to see what happens from a regulation in a UK perspective. And in terms of the work we are doing on balance sheet velocity, that would just give us an ability to be able to participate more without having that increase in RWAs and follow-through. I think we should all be pleased. We've been talking for years that we are going to have low-single-digit loan growth, and then we said we're not even going to talk about loan growth - and when you stop talking about it, it starts, so we just have to see how it plays out.
data.reason: The answer directly addresses the question's intent, covering competitive dynamics, balance sheet demand, and product margins in CIB, and the impact of US and UK capital regulations. It provides a medium level of evidence with some concrete support but lacks numeric evidence.
